name: Introduction to Business Concepts
notes: Competency areas and weighting from the National FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Introduction to Business Concepts (updated Aug 2026), as hosted by PA FBLA: https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/26-27-Introduction-to-Business-Concepts-PA.pdf . The 2025-26 PDF was not reachable (NYS copy returned 404, fbla.org returned 403), so the 2026-27 areas are used; the knowledge-area list is the same family of areas. The guideline lists 100 multiple-choice questions in 50 minutes. The printed weights (30/25/20/15/10/5) do not map cleanly to the eight areas in text extraction, so per-area question counts are an approximate split (20/15/15/16/14/10/5/5). Tests use U.S. conventions.

questions.q: Which term describes the condition in which unlimited human wants exceed limited resources?
questions.explain: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: resources are limited relative to wants, which forces choices. Surplus is a market condition, not the underlying problem.

questions.q: Maria can either work a shift that pays $80 or attend a training course. She chooses the course. What is her opportunity cost of the course?
choices: The full cost of the training course
The $80 of pay she gave up by not working the shift
Zero, since the course is free
The total of all her possible earnings for the year
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, not the price paid. The trap is confusing it with out-of-pocket cost.

questions.q: A product's price rises from $20 to $25. What is the percentage increase?
questions.explain: The change is $5 on a base of $20, so $5 / $20 = 25%. A common error is dividing by the new price.

questions.q: Which change would shift the demand curve for a normal good to the right?
choices: A decrease in the good's own price
An increase in the good's own price
A rise in the cost of raw materials
questions.explain: Income changes shift demand; a change in the good's own price only moves along the existing curve. Raw material costs affect supply, not demand.

questions.q: Which change would shift the supply curve for a product to the right?
choices: A decrease in the cost of raw materials
An increase in consumer preference for the product
A rise in the product's own price
questions.explain: Lower input costs let firms produce more at every price, shifting supply right. Consumer preferences and income affect demand.

questions.q: Which factor of production is human effort, both physical and mental, used to produce goods and services?
questions.explain: Labor is the human work input. Capital is human-made goods, land is natural resources, and entrepreneurship is risk-taking and organizing.

questions.q: Which factor of production is the willingness to take on risk and combine the other resources to pursue profit?
questions.explain: Entrepreneurship is the fourth factor of production, and it is the factor that organizes and bears risk.

questions.q: In economics, which of the following best describes capital as a factor of production?
choices: Money held in a bank account
Natural resources such as timber and water
Human-made goods, such as machinery and tools, used to produce other goods
questions.explain: Economic capital means produced goods used in production. Money is financial capital and is not counted as a factor of production in the classic model.

questions.q: Which measure best describes gross domestic product (GDP)?
choices: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period
The total income earned by citizens living abroad
The total value of all goods a country imports
The total money supply in circulation
questions.explain: GDP measures production within the borders of a country over a time period. Income earned abroad and imports are different measures.

questions.q: What term describes a sustained, general increase in the price level of goods and services?
questions.explain: Inflation is a broad, persistent rise in prices. Deflation is the opposite, and depreciation refers to an asset losing value.

questions.q: A basket of goods costs $400 last year and $420 this year. What is the rate of inflation?
questions.explain: The change is $20 divided by last year's $400 base, which equals 5%. Dividing by this year's $420 gives the 4.76% trap.

questions.q: At market equilibrium, which condition holds?
choices: Price is at its highest possible level
The government has set a price ceiling
questions.explain: Equilibrium is where the supply and demand curves intersect, so quantity demanded equals quantity supplied and there is no pressure to change price.

questions.q: When the price of a good is above its equilibrium level, what typically happens?
choices: A surplus forms, which puts downward pressure on price
A shortage forms, which puts upward pressure on price
A surplus forms, which puts upward pressure on price
A shortage forms with no pressure on price
questions.explain: At a price above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, creating a surplus. The unsold stock pushes the price down toward equilibrium.

questions.q: A business owner can earn $50,000 running her current company or $35,000 teaching. If she runs the company, what is her opportunity cost?
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative, here $35,000. The $50,000 is what she gains, not what she gives up.

questions.q: Country A can make a unit of cloth at a lower opportunity cost than Country B. Which statement is correct?
choices: Country A has an absolute advantage in every good
Country A has no advantage in cloth
Country A has a comparative advantage in producing cloth
Country A always wins in trade due to lower wages
questions.explain: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, not on absolute output or wages. A country can hold a comparative advantage even if it is not the most productive at everything.

questions.q: A 10% increase in price causes a 20% decrease in quantity demanded. Demand for this good is:
choices: Inelastic, because quantity fell by more than price rose
Unit elastic, because the two percentages are close
Elastic, because the elasticity ratio is greater than 1
questions.explain: Elasticity is the percent change in quantity divided by the percent change in price, here 20% / 10% = 2. A ratio above 1 means demand is elastic.

questions.q: Which market structure has many sellers, identical products, and free entry and exit?
questions.explain: Perfect competition assumes identical products and free entry. Monopolistic competition has differentiated products, so it is the closest distractor.

questions.q: Which phase of the business cycle is characterized by falling real GDP and rising unemployment?
questions.explain: Contraction is the downturn phase. Recovery is the rise after a trough, and expansion is the growth phase, so both are traps.

questions.q: A worker quits a job to look for a better position and is between jobs for two months. This is an example of which type of unemployment?
questions.explain: Frictional unemployment is short-term and comes from workers moving between jobs. Structural unemployment comes from skill mismatches, and cyclical comes from downturns.

questions.q: When the Federal Reserve raises the federal funds rate, which outcome is most likely?
choices: The money supply rises and spending increases
Inflation automatically rises to offset the change
Borrowing becomes more expensive and spending tends to slow
questions.explain: A higher policy rate raises borrowing costs across the economy, which slows spending and can cool inflation. Its effects are indirect and take time.

questions.q: Which form of business ownership offers no legal separation between the owner's personal and business liabilities?
questions.explain: A sole proprietor and the business are one legal person, so the owner is personally liable for business debts.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of a corporation over a sole proprietorship?
choices: Owners are personally liable for all business debts
It is the simplest and cheapest form to form
Profits are taxed only once at the owner's personal rate
questions.explain: Shareholders are generally not personally liable for corporate debts. Corporations are more costly to form and may face double taxation.

questions.q: Which business structure is most associated with double taxation of profits?
questions.explain: A C corporation pays tax on profits, and shareholders pay tax again on dividends. An S corporation passes income through to owners and avoids this.

questions.q: In a general partnership, what is the usual liability of each partner for business debts?
choices: Liable only up to the amount they invested
Not liable for debts incurred by other partners
Jointly and severally liable, so a creditor can pursue any partner for the full amount
questions.explain: General partners are personally liable for partnership debts, and each partner can be held responsible for the full amount. Limited liability is a feature of LLCs and corporations.

questions.q: Which group is a stakeholder in a business but is not necessarily a shareholder?
questions.explain: Stakeholders include anyone affected by the business, such as employees, customers, and communities. Shareholders are only one stakeholder group.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a company's mission statement?
choices: To forecast revenue for the next five years
To communicate the organization's core purpose and reason for existing
To list the company's main competitors
To set the quarterly financial targets
questions.explain: A mission statement explains why the organization exists. Forecasts, competitors, and targets belong in other planning documents.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, which element refers to external factors that could help the business?
questions.explain: Opportunities are external conditions the business can exploit. Strengths are internal, and threats are external but harmful.

questions.q: How is net profit calculated?
choices: Gross sales minus cost of goods sold
Total revenue divided by total expenses
questions.explain: Net profit is the bottom line after all expenses. Gross sales minus cost of goods sold gives gross profit, and assets minus liabilities gives equity.

questions.q: Which action best demonstrates corporate social responsibility?
choices: Voluntarily cutting the factory's emissions below what the law requires
Hiding a product defect to protect sales
Moving operations overseas solely to avoid all local laws
Paying the lowest wage the market will bear without any review
questions.explain: CSR means taking responsibility for social and environmental impact beyond legal minimums. Hiding defects and evading laws are unethical choices.

questions.q: A person buys the right to operate a business using an established company's brand and operating system. This person is a:
questions.explain: The franchisee pays fees and royalties to use the franchisor's brand and system. The franchisor is the company granting the rights.

questions.q: What distinguishes a limited liability company (LLC) from a general partnership?
choices: LLCs cannot have more than one owner
LLCs must issue shares of stock to the public
LLC members generally have limited liability for business debts
LLC profits are always taxed at the corporate rate
questions.explain: An LLC combines limited liability with flexible tax treatment. A general partnership has no such shield, and LLCs can have multiple owners and do not issue public stock by default.

questions.q: In a business plan, which section describes target customers and competitors?
questions.explain: The market analysis section covers the target market, customer needs, and competition. The executive summary is an overview placed at the front.

questions.q: Which term describes a person who organizes, operates, and assumes the risks of a business?
questions.explain: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and bears its risk. An investor provides capital but may not operate the business.

questions.q: A company has $240,000 in revenue and $180,000 in total expenses. What is its net profit margin?
questions.explain: Net profit is $60,000 and the margin is $60,000 / $240,000 = 25%. Dividing by expenses gives the 33.3% trap, and $60,000 is profit, not a margin.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of buying a franchise for the franchisee?
choices: Full control over menu and pricing decisions
Access to an established brand and a proven business system
questions.explain: Franchisees gain brand recognition and a tested system, but they pay fees and follow standards. Full control and fee-free operation are not typical benefits.

questions.q: Which economic system uses customs, beliefs, and history to decide what is produced?
questions.explain: A traditional economy relies on long-standing customs and roles. Command economies use central planning, and market economies use prices.

questions.q: In a command economy, who primarily decides what goods are produced?
questions.explain: In a command economy, a central authority plans production and allocation. The other options describe market mechanisms.

questions.q: A mixed economy is best described as:
choices: Equal government ownership of every business
A combination of market forces and government intervention
A system with no private property at all
questions.explain: Mixed economies combine private enterprise with government regulation or public services. Pure systems are rare.

questions.q: Which characteristic is most central to a market economy?
choices: Private ownership of resources, with prices set by supply and demand
questions.explain: Market economies rely on private ownership and price signals. The other options describe command or traditional systems.

questions.q: The transfer of a government-owned business to private ownership is called:
questions.explain: Privatization moves a public enterprise into private hands. Nationalization is the reverse, and deregulation removes rules without changing ownership.

questions.q: Which U.S. federal law is the primary statute prohibiting monopolies and restraints of trade?
questions.explain: The Sherman Act is the foundational U.S. antitrust law. The other laws cover securities, wages, and consumer credit.

questions.q: Which concept, introduced by Adam Smith, describes self-interested individuals unintentionally advancing society's welfare?
questions.explain: Smith's invisible hand describes how self-interest in competitive markets can benefit society. The other concepts describe different economic ideas.

questions.q: Which characteristic is most associated with socialism?
choices: Unrestricted private ownership of all businesses
Prices set only by bidding between consumers
Significant collective or government ownership of major means of production
No public services provided to citizens
questions.explain: Socialism emphasizes collective ownership of major industries. Private ownership and limited public services are the opposite.

questions.q: When shared, unowned resources are overused and depleted, economists call this:
questions.explain: Shared resources with no clear owner tend to be overused. Free riding, moral hazard, and adverse selection are different market problems.

questions.q: Which government action is a consumer-protection regulation?
choices: Requiring food labels to list ingredients and allergens
Imposing a tariff on imported steel
Giving a tax credit to solar panel manufacturers
questions.explain: Labeling rules protect consumers from harm and deception. Subsidies and tariffs are economic policy tools, not consumer protection.

questions.q: A tax on imported goods is called a:
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports. A quota limits quantity, a subsidy pays producers, and an embargo bans trade.

questions.q: A government payment to a producer to lower its production costs is called a:
questions.explain: Subsidies reduce a producer's costs or increase its revenue. Tariffs and excise taxes raise money, and a price ceiling caps prices.

questions.q: Command economies are most likely to experience which problem?
choices: Shortages and surpluses caused by planners misjudging demand
questions.explain: Without price signals, central planners often misallocate goods, causing shortages or surpluses. Private property and competition are features of market systems.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why pure market economies rarely exist in practice?
choices: Governments usually provide public goods, regulate externalities, and redistribute income
Consumers never have enough information to buy anything
Markets always produce too many goods
Private firms are legally barred from earning profits
questions.explain: Public goods, externalities, and inequality are market failures that most governments address, so real systems are mixed.

questions.q: Which term describes a cost or benefit imposed on people who are not part of a transaction?
questions.explain: An externality affects third parties, such as pollution from a factory. A public good is non-excludable, and monopsony is a single buyer.

questions.q: Which cost does NOT change with the level of production in the short run?
questions.explain: Fixed costs such as rent stay the same regardless of output. The other costs rise as production rises.

questions.q: Which cost is a variable cost for a bakery?
questions.explain: Variable costs change with output, and flour per batch rises with production. The others are fixed in the short run.

questions.q: A business has fixed costs of $12,000, a price of $40 per unit, and variable cost of $25 per unit. How many units must it sell to break even?
questions.explain: Contribution margin is $40 - $25 = $15, and $12,000 / $15 = 800 units. Dividing fixed costs by price (300) is a common mistake.

questions.q: Sales are $150,000 and cost of goods sold is $90,000. What is gross profit?
questions.explain: Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold, so $150,000 - $90,000 = $60,000.

questions.q: A retailer buys an item for $50 and sells it for $75. What is the markup as a percentage of cost?
questions.explain: Markup on cost is ($75 - $50) / $50 = 50%. The 33.3% figure is the gross margin, which divides by the selling price.

questions.q: Fixed costs are $5,000, and variable cost is $8 per unit. What is total cost of producing 1,000 units?
questions.explain: Total cost = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x units) = $5,000 + $8,000 = $13,000.

questions.q: A product sells for $30 and has variable cost of $18 per unit. What is its contribution margin per unit?
questions.explain: Contribution margin is price minus variable cost per unit, here $30 - $18 = $12. It is the amount each sale contributes toward fixed costs.

questions.q: Which term refers to total revenue minus all costs, including taxes and interest?
questions.explain: Net income is the bottom line after every expense. Gross profit excludes operating costs, and operating income excludes interest and taxes.

questions.q: Marginal cost is best defined as:
choices: The average cost across all units produced
Total fixed cost divided by output
The additional cost of producing one more unit
The cost of the most recent inventory purchase
questions.explain: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit. Average cost spreads total cost over all units.

questions.q: At the break-even point, a business's:
questions.explain: Break-even occurs where revenue covers all costs, so profit is zero. Fixed costs never fall to zero at this point.

questions.q: Which costs are included in cost of goods sold for a manufacturer?
choices: Direct materials, direct labor, and factory overhead
questions.explain: COGS covers costs of making the product sold. Selling, administrative, and financing costs are reported separately as operating or other expenses.

questions.q: Which pricing strategy sets a low introductory price to gain market share quickly?
questions.explain: Penetration pricing starts low to attract buyers and build share. Skimming starts high and lowers price over time.

questions.q: As a firm increases output, its average cost per unit falls because of:
questions.explain: Spreading fixed costs over more units and using efficient processes lowers average cost. Diseconomies raise it, and diminishing returns are a short-run production concept.

questions.q: Operating expenses are $35,000 and gross profit is $80,000. What is operating income?
questions.explain: Operating income = gross profit - operating expenses = $80,000 - $35,000 = $45,000.

questions.q: Fixed costs are $60,000 and the contribution margin ratio is 40%. What are break-even sales in dollars?
questions.explain: Break-even sales = fixed costs / contribution margin ratio = $60,000 / 0.40 = $150,000. Multiplying instead of dividing gives the $24,000 trap.

questions.q: Which change would LOWER a firm's break-even point in units?
choices: A higher selling price with costs unchanged
An increase in variable cost per unit
questions.explain: A higher price raises the contribution margin per unit, so fewer units are needed to cover fixed costs. The other options raise the break-even point.

questions.q: What is a key disadvantage of raising money through equity rather than debt?
choices: The business must make fixed loan payments
Lenders can claim business assets if payments are missed
Owners give up part of the ownership and future profits
questions.explain: Equity investors share ownership and profits, which dilutes the owner's control. The other options describe disadvantages of debt.

questions.q: Which equation is the basic accounting equation?
questions.explain: The accounting equation states that a company's assets are financed by liabilities and owner's equity. The other forms are incorrect.

questions.q: Which financial statement reports revenues and expenses over a period of time?
questions.explain: The income statement summarizes performance over a period. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date.

questions.q: A business is profitable on paper but runs out of money and fails. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Profit is an accounting measure, and cash flow is the timing of actual money. A profitable firm can still fail if cash runs out.

questions.q: What does the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) typically do for small business loans?
choices: Lends directly to all small businesses at zero interest
Buys shares in small businesses on the public market
Guarantees a portion of loans made by approved lenders
Sets interest rates on all commercial loans
questions.explain: SBA loan programs reduce lender risk by guaranteeing part of a loan made by a bank. The SBA is not the direct lender in most programs.

questions.q: Which description best fits an angel investor?
choices: A bank that offers government-backed loans
A firm pooling money to buy shares of mature public companies
A government agency that provides grants
An individual who invests personal funds in early-stage businesses
questions.explain: Angel investors are individuals funding young companies, often in exchange for equity. The other options describe lenders or public market investors.

questions.q: The primary purpose of a business plan is to:
choices: Guide the business and communicate its strategy and financial projections
Report past taxes to the government
Replace the need for an accounting system
questions.explain: A business plan is a planning and communication tool for owners, lenders, and investors. It does not replace accounting or legal filings.

questions.q: Which insurance covers claims that a customer was injured by the business's product?
questions.explain: Product liability insurance covers claims from product-related injuries. The others cover lost income, a key employee's loss, or employee injuries.

questions.q: A company has current assets of $180,000 and current liabilities of $90,000. What is its current ratio?
questions.explain: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, so $180,000 / $90,000 = 2.0. Inverting the ratio gives 0.5 to 1.

questions.q: Working capital is calculated as:
choices: Total revenue minus cost of goods sold
questions.explain: Working capital measures short-term liquidity. Total assets minus total liabilities is net worth, and the other options are different measures.

questions.q: A small business needs $25,000 for equipment to be repaid over five years. Which financing is most appropriate?
choices: A line of credit for daily expenses
Issuing common stock in an initial public offering
questions.explain: A term loan provides a lump sum repaid on a fixed schedule, which matches a long-term asset. Lines of credit and trade credit suit short-term needs.

questions.q: A company buys equipment for $50,000 with a five-year life and no salvage value, using straight-line depreciation. What is the annual depreciation expense?
questions.explain: Straight-line depreciation spreads the cost evenly: $50,000 / 5 = $10,000 per year.

questions.q: Which is the best description of a business line of credit?
choices: A fixed loan repaid in equal installments over ten years
An investment in exchange for an ownership stake
A revolving loan up to a set limit, borrowed and repaid as needed
A grant that never has to be repaid
questions.explain: A line of credit lets the business draw and repay within a limit, which suits fluctuating cash needs. Fixed installment loans and equity investments work differently.

questions.q: Which metric shows how much of a company's financing comes from creditors relative to owners?
questions.explain: Debt-to-equity compares total liabilities to owner's equity. The other ratios measure liquidity, profitability, or efficiency.

questions.q: A farm that grows wheat is part of which sector of the economy?
questions.explain: The primary sector extracts or grows natural resources, such as farming, mining, and fishing.

questions.q: A factory that assembles cars is classified in which sector?
questions.explain: The secondary sector transforms raw materials into finished goods through manufacturing.

questions.q: A bank that makes loans to customers is part of which sector?
questions.explain: The tertiary sector provides services. Banking, retail, and transportation all fall here.

questions.q: A business buys goods in bulk from manufacturers and sells them to retailers. It is a:
questions.explain: Wholesalers sell to businesses rather than final consumers. Retailers sell directly to consumers.

questions.q: A software company sells accounting software to other businesses. Its activity is primarily:
questions.explain: B2B means selling to other businesses. B2C is selling to individual consumers.

questions.q: Which description best defines e-commerce?
choices: Offline sales of goods in physical stores
Buying and selling goods or services over the internet
questions.explain: E-commerce is any commercial transaction conducted electronically. It does not require a physical store.

questions.q: What defines a nonprofit organization?
choices: It is not allowed to earn any revenue
It is owned by shareholders who receive dividends
It reinvests surplus revenue into its mission instead of paying profits to owners
It is automatically exempt from all taxes
questions.explain: Nonprofits can earn revenue but cannot distribute profits to owners. Tax-exempt status must be applied for and is not automatic.

questions.q: Members of a cooperative are typically:
choices: Outside investors with no voting rights
Government appointees who run the business
Owners who share in the business's profits or benefits
questions.explain: Cooperatives are owned and governed by their members, who share in the benefits. The other options describe other structures.

questions.q: Which of the following is a pure service business?
questions.explain: A pure service business sells expertise or labor rather than physical goods. The others are primary or secondary producers.

questions.q: What does a franchisor typically earn from its franchise system?
choices: Profit from reselling inventory to franchisees at cost
Royalties and franchise fees paid by franchisees
Full sales revenue from every outlet it owns
Membership charges paid directly by customers
questions.explain: Franchisors earn ongoing royalties and initial fees rather than the sales of each outlet. The other options describe models the franchisor does not usually use.

questions.q: Which section of a resume lists relevant work history, usually in reverse chronological order?
questions.explain: Professional experience shows what the candidate has done, with the most recent job first. References are listed separately.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a cover letter?
choices: To list every duty from your past roles
To provide a complete record of your education
To request a salary before the interview
To introduce yourself and explain your fit for a specific job
questions.explain: A cover letter tailors the application to one role and highlights the most relevant qualifications. It does not repeat the resume.

questions.q: Which is an example of professional networking?
choices: Connecting with an alumnus in your field to ask for an informational interview
Posting personal photos on social media for employers to see
Asking a classmate to write a fake reference
Sending unsolicited mass emails to every company in a state
questions.explain: Networking builds relationships for career information and opportunities. Fabricated references and mass unsolicited emails are not effective or ethical networking.

questions.q: What should come FIRST when creating a career plan?
choices: Assessing your interests, skills, and values
Accepting the first offer you receive
Memorizing answers to common interview questions
questions.explain: Self-assessment comes first, because goals and job targets depend on interests, skills, and values. The other steps come later.

questions.q: Which characteristic makes a career goal a SMART goal?
choices: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound
questions.explain: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound, which makes progress trackable. The other options do not match the acronym.

questions.q: In the STAR interview method, what does the letter 'A' stand for?
questions.explain: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, and Result. Candidates describe what they did, then the outcome.

questions.q: How soon after an interview should a candidate typically send a thank-you note?
choices: Only if the employer asks for one
questions.explain: A prompt thank-you note, usually within 24 hours, reinforces interest. Waiting a month or sending it beforehand is ineffective.

questions.q: When listing references on a job application, what should you do first?
choices: Ask each person's permission before listing them
Include home addresses for every reference
Submit a new list only after the employer asks for one
questions.explain: Asking permission ensures references are willing and prepared to speak. Listing people without asking can harm the application.

questions.q: Why do many employers use applicant tracking systems (ATS) to screen resumes?
choices: To verify applicants' social security numbers
To scan for keywords that match the job description
To eliminate any resume without a photo
questions.explain: An ATS filters resumes by matching keywords from the job posting, so tailoring resumes to the description matters. It does not check identity or age.

questions.q: Which element of a job posting describes the duties and expectations of the role?
questions.explain: The job description lists responsibilities and expectations. The title names the role, but it does not describe duties in detail.

vocab.def: The condition in which unlimited wants exceed the limited resources available to satisfy them.
The value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
The quantity of a good producers are willing and able to offer at various prices during a period.
The quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices during a period.
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no pressure to change it.
A sustained general increase in the price level of goods and services over time.
The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
The inputs used to produce goods and services: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
A measure of how much quantity demanded or supplied responds to a change in price.
The phase of the business cycle in which real GDP declines and economic activity slows.
Actions by a central bank, such as changing interest rates, to influence the money supply and economic activity.
A business owned and run by one person, with no legal separation between owner and business.
A business owned by two or more people who share profits, losses, and management.
A legal entity separate from its owners, which gives shareholders limited liability.
A business structure that offers owners limited liability and flexible pass-through tax treatment.
Any person or group affected by a business's decisions, such as employees, customers, or the community.
A statement that describes an organization's core purpose and reason for existing.
A business arrangement in which a franchisee pays fees to operate under a franchisor's brand and system.
A person who organizes, operates, and assumes the risks of a business in pursuit of profit.
A planning tool that assesses a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
An economic system in which customs, beliefs, and history determine what is produced and how.
An economic system in which a central government plans and directs production and distribution.
An economic system in which private individuals own resources and prices are set by supply and demand.
An economic system combining market forces with significant government intervention.
An economic system with significant collective or government ownership of major means of production.
The transfer of a government-owned business or asset to private ownership.
A tax imposed on imported goods.
A cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on people who are not part of it.
Adam Smith's term for how self-interested decisions in competitive markets can benefit society as a whole.
A business cost that does not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent.
A business cost that rises or falls with the level of output, such as materials used in production.
The level of sales at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero.
Sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold.
The amount added to the cost of a product to set its selling price, often expressed as a percentage of cost.
The selling price per unit minus the variable cost per unit, which contributes toward fixed costs.
Total revenue minus all expenses, including operating costs, interest, and taxes.
The additional cost of producing one more unit of output.
Cost advantages that lower average cost per unit as a firm increases its output.
A written document that describes a business's goals, strategy, market, and financial projections.
Raising money by selling ownership shares in the business.
Raising money by borrowing, which must be repaid with interest.
